items.text: Longformer’s memory usage scales linearly with the sequence length, unlike the full self-attention mechanism that runs out of memory for long sequences on current GPUs.
items.why: States memory scaling vs. standard self-attention.
items.plain: Longformer uses memory that grows linearly with sequence length, whereas standard self-attention runs out of memory on current graphics processing units when given long text sequences.

items.text: Longformer’s attention mechanism is a combination of a windowed local-context self-attention and an end task motivated global attention that encodes inductive bias about the task.
items.why: Deﬁnes the core attention mechanism design.
items.plain: Longformer combines local windowed self-attention with a task-specific global attention pattern.

items.text: Through ablations and controlled trials we show both attention types are essential – the local attention is primarily used to build contextual representations, while the global attention allows Longformer to build full sequence representations for prediction.
items.why: Explains the functional roles of local and global attention.
items.plain: Local attention builds representations from nearby tokens, while global attention lets the model build a representation of the entire sequence for final predictions.

items.text: Then, to evaluate Longformer’s ability to replace the full self-attention operation of existing pretrained models, we pretrain it with the masked language modeling (MLM) objective, continuing from the RoBERTa (Liu et al., 2019) released checkpoint.
items.why: Explains the pretraining strategy using RoBERTa.
items.plain: To test whether it can replace standard self-attention, the authors pretrain Longformer using masked language modeling, starting from the released RoBERTa weights.

items.text: To address this challenge, we sparsify the full self-attention matrix according to an “attention pattern” specifying pairs of input locations attending to one another.
items.why: States how self-attention is sparsified into a pattern.
items.plain: The full self-attention matrix is made sparse by defining specific pairs of input positions that attend to one another.

items.text: Sliding Window Given the importance of local context (Kovaleva et al., 2019), our attention pattern employs a ﬁxed-size window attention surrounding each token.
items.why: Defines the sliding window attention design.
items.plain: The attention pattern uses a fixed-size window around each token to capture local context.

items.text: Given a ﬁxed window size w, each token attends to 1
items.why: Defines token attention range under the sliding window.
items.plain: With a fixed window size w, each token attends to a fraction of its neighboring tokens on each side.

items.text: The computation complexity of this pattern is O(n × w),
items.why: Gives the computational complexity of sliding window attention.
items.plain: The computational complexity of sliding window attention is O(n × w), where n is the sequence length and w is the window size.

items.text: In a transformer with ℓlayers, the receptive ﬁeld size at the top layer is ℓ× w (assuming w is ﬁxed for all layers).
items.why: Gives the top-layer receptive field size formula.
items.plain: In an l-layer transformer with a fixed window size w, the top layer has a receptive field size of l × w.

items.text: Dilated Sliding Window To further increase the receptive ﬁeld without increasing computation, the sliding window can be “dilated”.
items.why: Defines the dilated sliding window attention.
items.plain: The sliding window can be dilated to increase its receptive field without adding computational cost.

items.text: Assuming a ﬁxed d and w for all layers, the receptive ﬁeld is ℓ× d × w, which can reach tens of thousands of tokens even for small values of d.
items.why: Gives the receptive field formula for dilated windows.
items.plain: If dilation d and window size w are fixed across all layers, the top-layer receptive field becomes l × d × w.

items.text: We found settings with different dilation conﬁgurations per head improves performance by allowing some heads without dilation to focus on local context, while others with dilation focus on longer context.
items.why: Describes per-head dilation configurations.
items.plain: Using different dilation settings across attention heads improves performance because some heads focus on local context while others focus on longer context.

items.text: Accordingly, we add “global attention” on few pre-selected input locations.
items.why: Explains why and where global attention is added.
items.plain: Global attention is added to a small set of pre-selected input positions to learn task-specific representations.

items.text: Importantly, we make this attention operation symmetric: that is, a token with a global attention attends to all tokens across the sequence, and all tokens in the sequence attend to it.
items.why: Defines the symmetric property of global attention.
items.plain: Global attention is symmetric: tokens assigned global attention attend to all sequence tokens, and every sequence token attends back to them.

items.text: For example for classiﬁcation, global attention is used for the [CLS] token while in QA global attention is provided on all question tokens.
items.why: Gives task-specific examples of global attention locations.
items.plain: For text classification, global attention is placed on the [CLS] token, whereas for question answering, it is placed on all question tokens.

items.text: Since the number of such tokens is small relative to and independent of n the complexity of the combined local and global attention is still O(n).
items.why: Explains why combined local and global attention remains linear.
items.plain: Because the number of global tokens is small and independent of the sequence length n, the combined local and global attention complexity remains O(n).

items.text: We use two sets of projections, Qs, Ks, Vs to com-
items.why: Describes separate query, key, and value projection sets.
items.plain: The model uses separate sets of query, key, and value linear projections for sliding window attention versus global attention.

items.text: Qg, Kg, Vg are all initialized with values that match Qs, Ks, Vs.
items.why: States how global attention projections are initialized.
items.plain: The linear projections for global attention are initialized with values copied from the sliding window attention projections.

items.text: For Longformer, the dilated sliding window attention computes only a ﬁxed number of the diagonals of QKT .
items.why: Explains the matrix operation calculated by dilated attention.
items.plain: Dilated sliding window attention computes only a fixed set of diagonals from the full matrix multiplication of queries and keys.

items.text: Fig. 1 compares the performance of three different ways of implementing it: loop is a memory efﬁcient Py- Torch implementation that supports dilation but is unusably slow and only used for testing; chunks only supports the non-dilated case and is used for the pretraining/ﬁnetuning setting; and cuda is our fully functioning highly optimized custom CUDA kernel implemented using TVM (Chen et al., 2018) and used for the language modeling experiments (see Appendix A for more details).
items.why: Summarizes implementation options for the custom CUDA kernel.
items.plain: The authors compare three implementation approaches: a slow loop version for testing, a chunked vectorized version for non-dilated pretraining and fine-tuning, and a fast custom CUDA kernel built with TVM for language modeling.

items.text: Following Sukhbaatar et al. (2019) we use differing window sizes across the layers.
items.why: Describes layer-wise window sizes for language modeling.
items.plain: For language modeling, the model uses smaller window sizes in lower layers and larger window sizes in higher layers.

items.text: We do not use dilated sliding windows for lower layers to maximize their capacity to learn and utilize the immediate local context.
items.why: States where dilation is omitted in language modeling.
items.plain: Lower layers do not use dilated sliding windows so they can focus on capturing immediate local context.

items.text: For the higher layers, we use a small amount of increasing dilation only on 2 heads.
items.why: States how dilation is applied in higher layers.
items.plain: Higher layers use a small amount of increasing dilation on only two attention heads.

items.text: To accommodate this, we adopt a staged training procedure where we increase the attention window size and sequence length across multiple training phases.
items.why: Describes the staged training strategy across sequence lengths.
items.plain: Training uses a staged procedure that gradually increases the attention window size and sequence length across multiple phases.

items.text: In particular, in the ﬁrst phase we start with a short sequence length and window size, then on each subsequent phase, we double the window size and the sequence length, and halve the learning rate.
items.why: Specifies how hyperparameters change during staged training phases.
items.plain: Each subsequent training phase doubles the sequence length and window size while halving the learning rate.

items.text: We train the model over 5 total phases with start-
items.why: Gives sequence length bounds across training phases.
items.plain: The model is trained across five total phases, starting at a sequence length of 2,048 tokens and ending at 23,040 tokens.

items.text: We achieve a new state-of-the-art on both text8 and enwik8 using the small models with BPC of 1.10 and 1.00 on text8 and enwik8 respectively, demonstrating the effectiveness of our model.
items.why: States character language modeling benchmark results.
items.plain: Small Longformer models achieve state-of-the-art bits-per-character scores of 1.10 on text8 and 1.00 on enwik8.

items.text: Tab. 3 shows that Longformer outperforms the comparable Transformer- XL model, matches the performance of the comparable Sparse Transformer (Child et al., 2019), and matches or slightly underperforms recent models that have more than twice the number of parameters.
items.why: Summarizes performance of large Longformer models on enwik8.
items.plain: On enwik8, large Longformer models outperform comparable Transformer-XL models, match Sparse Transformers, and perform similarly to models with over twice as many parameters.

items.text: We observe that increasing the window size from the bottom to the top layer leads to the best performance, arranging them in the reverse way leads to worse performance, and using a ﬁxed window size (the average of window sizes of the other conﬁguration) leads to a performance that it is in between.
items.why: Reports ablation findings on layer-wise window sizing.
items.plain: Increasing window sizes from lower to higher layers yields the best performance, outperforming fixed or decreasing window size arrangements.

items.text: Adding some dilation to two heads leads to some improvement compared with no dilation at all.
items.why: Reports ablation findings on adding dilation.
items.plain: Adding dilation to two attention heads improves performance compared to using no dilation.

items.text: The resulting model can process sequences up to 4,096 tokens long (8 times longer than BERT)5.
items.why: States maximum sequence capacity after pretraining.
items.plain: The pretrained Longformer can process input sequences up to 4,096 tokens long.

items.text: Attention Pattern We use sliding window attention with window size of 512, therefore using the same amount of computation as RoBERTa.6
items.why: Gives pretraining window size to equal RoBERTa compute.
items.plain: Pretraining uses a sliding window size of 512 tokens to match the computation of RoBERTa.

items.text: To support longer documents, we add extra position embeddings to support up to position 4,096.
items.why: Explains how position embeddings are extended to 4096.
items.plain: The authors add extra position embeddings to extend the maximum sequence length from 512 to 4,096 tokens.

items.text: To leverage RoBERTa’s pretrained weights, instead of randomly initializing the new position embeddings, we initialize them by copying the 512 position embeddings from RoBERTa multiple times as analysis of BERT’s attention heads shows a strong learned bias to attending to local context, including the previous or next token (Clark et al., 2019).
items.why: Describes the copy initialization of extended position embeddings.
items.plain: New position embeddings are initialized by copying RoBERTa's 512 position embeddings multiple times instead of initializing them randomly.

items.text: Both models are trained for 65K gradient updates with sequences length 4,096, batch size 64 (218 tokens), maximum learning rate of 3e-5, linear warmup of 500 steps, followed by a power 3 polynomial decay.
items.why: States MLM pretraining hyperparameters and schedule.
items.plain: Base and large models are pretrained for 65,000 gradient updates on sequences of length 4,096 with a batch size of 64.

items.text: The signiﬁcant difference indicates the importance of the copy initialization, and the relative small difference between the RoBERTa BPC and the initialized BPC indicates that our sliding window attention is working well with the RoBERTa weights.
items.why: Shows the effect of position embedding copy initialization.
items.plain: Copy initialization significantly outperforms random initialization, showing that sliding window attention works well with RoBERTa's pretrained weights.

items.text: Traininig for 2K steps improves BPC from 1.957 to 1.753, which further decreases to 1.705 after 65K steps, demonstrating the model is learning to better utilize the sliding window attention and longer context.
items.why: Reports BPC improvements during continued MLM pretraining.
items.plain: Pretraining for 2,000 steps drops BPC from 1.957 to 1.753, and continuing to 65,000 steps further reduces it to 1.705.

items.text: This conﬁguration has a BPC of 1.850 (down from 1.957 at initialization), but higher than 1.705 where all the weights are trainable.
items.why: Reports results when freezing original RoBERTa weights.
items.plain: Freezing RoBERTa weights and training only new position embeddings yields a BPC of 1.850, which is worse than unfreezing all weights.

items.text: We include global attention to question tokens and answer candidates for WikiHop and to question tokens for TriviaQA.
items.why: Specifies global attention targets for WikiHop and TriviaQA.
items.plain: Global attention is assigned to question tokens and answer candidates for WikiHop, and to question tokens for TriviaQA.

items.text: We observe that Longformer consistently outperforms the RoBERTa baseline.
items.why: States main fine-tuning evaluation finding against RoBERTa.
items.plain: Longformer consistently outperforms the RoBERTa baseline across fine-tuning tasks.

items.text: Tab. 8 shows that our Longformer-large achieves new state-of-the-art results9 on WikiHop and TriviaQA by large margins (3.6 and 4 points respectively), and for HotpotQA, it underperforms the current state-of-the-art (Fang et al., 2020) by a point.
items.why: Reports state-of-the-art QA results for Longformer-large.
items.plain: Longformer-large achieves new state-of-the-art results on WikiHop and TriviaQA by 3.6 and 4 points respectively, while scoring slightly below state-of-the-art on HotpotQA.

items.text: Longformer beneﬁts from longer sequences, global attention, separate projection matrices for global attention, MLM pretraining, and longer training.
items.why: Summarizes key findings from WikiHop ablation studies.
items.plain: WikiHop performance improves with longer sequence lengths, global attention, separate global projection matrices, masked language model pretraining, and longer training.

items.text: To facilitate modeling long sequences for seq2seq learning, we propose a Longformer variant that has both the encoder and decoder Transformer stacks but instead of the full self-attention in the encoder, it uses the efﬁcient local+global attention pattern of the Longformer.
items.why: Defines the Longformer-Encoder-Decoder (LED) architecture.
items.plain: Longformer-Encoder-Decoder replaces full self-attention in the encoder with Longformer's local and global attention while maintaining a Transformer sequence-to-sequence structure.

items.text: The decoder uses the full self-attention to the entire encoded tokens and to previously decoded locations.
items.why: Describes decoder attention mechanism in LED.
items.plain: The LED decoder uses full self-attention over all encoded input tokens and previously generated output tokens.

items.text: The only difference is that to process longer inputs, we extend position embedding to 16K tokens (up from BART’s 1K tokens) and we initialize the new position embedding matrix by repeatedly copying BART’s 1K position embeddings 16 times as in Section 5 for RoBERTa.
items.why: Explains how LED position embeddings are initialized.
items.plain: LED extends position embeddings to 16,000 tokens by repeatedly copying BART's 1,000 position embeddings 16 times.

items.why: Reports LED summarization performance on arXiv dataset.
items.plain: LED-large with a 16,384 sequence length achieves ROUGE scores of 46.63 R-1, 19.62 R-2, and 41.83 R-L on the arXiv summarization dataset.

items.text: Longformer employs an attention pattern that combines local and global information while also scaling linearly with the sequence length.
items.why: Defines Longformer's key mechanism and scaling behavior.
items.plain: Longformer uses an attention mechanism that combines local and global context while scaling linearly with sequence length.

items.text: Implementing Longformer’s dilated sliding window attention requires a form of banded matrix multiplication (matrix multiplication where the output is all zero except certain diagonals) that is not directly supported in existing deep learning libraries like PyTorch/Tensorﬂow.
items.why: Explains the technical challenge in implementing the attention pattern.
items.plain: Implementing Longformer's dilated sliding window attention requires banded matrix multiplication, which standard deep learning libraries like PyTorch and TensorFlow do not natively support.

items.text: Longformer-loop is a naive implementation that computes each diagonal separately in a loop.
items.why: Describes the naive loop implementation method.
items.plain: The Longformer-loop implementation computes each matrix diagonal separately inside a loop.

items.text: It is memory efﬁcient because it only computes the non-zero values, but it is unusably slow.
items.why: States the trade-offs of the loop implementation.
items.plain: The loop method saves memory by computing only non-zero values, but it runs too slowly for practical use.

items.text: Longformer-chunks only supports the nondilated case.
items.why: Defines the scope of the chunked implementation.
items.plain: The Longformer-chunks implementation works only for attention patterns that do not use dilation.

items.text: It chunks Q and K into overlapping blocks of size w and overlap of size 1
items.why: Explains how the chunked implementation processes inputs.
items.plain: It breaks the Query and Key matrices into overlapping blocks of size w with a 0.5w overlap, multiplies those blocks, and then masks out the zeroed diagonals.

items.text: This is very compute efﬁcient because it uses a single matrix multiplication operation from PyTorch, but it consumes 2x the amount of memory a perfectly optimized implementation should consume because it computes some of the zero values.
items.why: States the trade-offs of the chunked implementation.
items.plain: This approach is compute-efficient because it uses standard PyTorch matrix multiplication, but it uses twice as much memory as an ideal implementation because it calculates some zero values.

items.text: Longformer-cuda is a custom CUDA kernel that we implement using TVM (Chen et al., 2018).
items.why: Introduces the custom CUDA implementation.
items.plain: Longformer-cuda is a custom GPU algorithm implemented using the Tensor Virtual Machine framework.

items.text: It is a fully functioning implementation of our attention (not limited as Longformer-chunks), it is the most memory efﬁcient, and it is as fast as the highly optimized full self-attention.10 We mainly use this implementation for the autoregressive language modeling experiments because of the memory efﬁciency (allows the longest sequences) and the support of dilation (needed for character- LM experiments).
items.why: Explains performance trade-offs and usage of the CUDA kernel.
items.plain: This implementation fully supports dilated and non-dilated attention, uses the least memory, runs as fast as full self-attention, and is used for autoregressive language modeling.

items.text: Using TVM, we describe our banded matrix multiplication in high-level python
items.why: Describes how the custom CUDA code is generated.
items.plain: The authors write the banded matrix multiplication in high-level Python, and TVM compiles it into optimized CUDA code for GPUs.

items.text: Our model only speciﬁes how the self-attention component works, and it is agnostic to the other design choices for the transformer model.
items.why: States modularity assumption regarding overall transformer architecture.
items.plain: The proposed method changes only the self-attention mechanism and can be used with any general Transformer design choices.

items.text: Our implementation is based on the Transformer-XL (Dai et al., 2019) code11 with the memory mechanism disabled.
items.why: Details the base codebase for character language modeling.
items.plain: The implementation is built on Transformer-XL code, but with its recurrence memory feature turned off.

items.text: We employed mixed precision training (ﬂoating points 16 and 32) using apex12 to reduce memory consumption and speed-up training.
items.why: Specifies numerical precision used for general model training.
items.plain: The authors used mixed 16-bit and 32-bit floating-point precision during training to reduce memory and increase speed.

items.text: However, we kept the attention computation in fp32 to avoid numerical instability issues.13 We used gradient checkpointing (Chen et al., 2016) to reduce memory usage, and ran our experiments on 48GB RTX8000 GPUs.
items.why: States numerical stability constraint and hardware setup.
items.plain: Attention calculations were kept in 32-bit floating point to prevent instability, while gradient checkpointing was used on 48GB RTX8000 GPUs.

items.text: Our CUDA kernel supports the autoregressive mode where each token attends to a window of previous tokens only.
items.why: Explains how the CUDA kernel supports autoregressive modeling.
items.plain: The custom GPU kernel supports autoregressive text generation by allowing each token to attend only to a sliding window of previous tokens.

items.text: Our implementation also includes a version of the relative position embedding that is compatible with our dilated sliding window attention.
items.why: Explains adaptation of position embeddings for dilated attention.
items.plain: The authors created a version of relative position embeddings that works with their dilated sliding window attention mechanism.

items.text: concatenate them to as much context as possible up to the model sequence length (512 for RoBERTa, 4,096 for Longformer), run the sequence through the model, collect the output activations, and repeat until all of the context is exhausted (for all models except Longformer-large, where we just include the ﬁrst 4,096 length sequence due to memory requirements).
items.why: Explains context processing and sequence limits for QA tasks.
items.plain: Questions and options are combined with context up to the maximum sequence length (512 for RoBERTa, 4,096 for Longformer) and run through the model in chunks if necessary.

items.text: In the case of Longformer, we use global attention to the entire question and answer candidate sequence.
items.why: Specifies global attention configuration for WikiHop.
items.plain: Longformer applies global attention to all tokens in the question and candidate answers.

items.text: We use global attention on all question tokens.
items.why: Specifies global attention placement for TriviaQA.
items.plain: Global attention is applied to all tokens in the question.

items.text: Our model for HotpotQA combines both answer span extraction and evidence extraction in one joint model.
items.why: Describes the joint multi-task design for HotpotQA.
items.plain: The HotpotQA model combines both answer text extraction and supporting evidence sentence identification into a single system.

items.text: We found a higher performance using a two-stage Longformer model with similar setup that ﬁrst identiﬁes relevant paragraphs and then does ﬁnd the ﬁnal answer span and evidence.15
items.why: Details two-stage pipeline enhancement for HotpotQA.
items.plain: A two-stage setup works better by using a first stage to select relevant paragraphs before running a second stage to find the answer span and evidence.

items.text: For Longformer, we use global attention to question tokens, paragraph title start tokens as well as sentence tokens.
items.why: Specifies global attention tokens for HotpotQA.
items.plain: Global attention is assigned to question tokens, paragraph title start tokens, and sentence tokens.

items.text: The maximum sequence length was 384 for RoBERTa-base, chosen after three trials from [256, 384, 512] using the default hyperparameters in the original implementation.16 For Longformer-base the sequence length was 4,096.
items.why: States sequence length difference between RoBERTa and Longformer.
items.plain: The maximum sequence length used was 384 for RoBERTa-base and 4,096 for Longformer-base.

items.text: Text classiﬁcation For classiﬁcation, following BERT, we used a simple binary cross entropy loss on top of a ﬁrst [CLS] token with addition of global attention to [CLS].
items.why: Describes text classification model setup and global attention.
items.plain: Text classification is performed by putting a binary cross-entropy loss layer on top of the initial token, which is set to use global attention.
